奎卡鼓屬膜鳴摩擦鼓，發聲來自內置木或竹棒經濕布摩擦，再以手指按壓鼓皮改變張力。其: The cuíca is a friction drum of the membranophone class; it sounds when the wooden or bamboo stick inside is rubbed with a damp cloth, and the player presses the drumhead with the fingers to change its tension. Its timbre is high and squeaky, and it is called the "laughing gourd"; its range is fairly large, and the degree of pressing adjusts both pitch and timbre. The source does not clearly state how volume is controlled. It is structurally close to similar friction drums such as the Portuguese sarronca and the Spanish zambomba; what distinguishes the cuíca is the high squeaky tone commonly heard in Brazilian carnival and samba.
奎卡鼓常見於巴西嘉年華與桑巴音樂，里約熱內盧嘉年華團體設有整排演奏者。它也用於民: The cuíca is common in Brazilian carnival and samba, and Rio de Janeiro carnival groups field a whole row of players. It also accompanies folk and urban popular dance, such as the Holy Cross dance at Santa Cruz in California in May, the Mozambico dramatic dance of Minas Gerais, the Holy Cross festival dances and processions, and samba performances in rural São Paulo. In radio-oriented samba, when no player is available, the singer or other musicians imitate its sound with the voice. It also appears on "Chega de Saudade", played by Dizzy Gillespie and composed by Antônio Carlos Jobim, and in jazz-rock, free jazz and Latin jazz line-ups.

The cuíca is a Brazilian friction drum, a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 231.11. The body is mostly metal, gourd or synthetic material, and a wooden or bamboo stick is fixed at the centre of the single animal-skin head, standing perpendicular to it. The player carries the drum under the arm against the chest on a shoulder strap, rubs the rosined stick up and down with a damp cloth in one hand, and presses the drumhead with the fingers of the other to change pitch and timbre. It is often used in carnival, samba and various folk and urban popular dances, such as the Rio de Janeiro carnival, rural São Paulo samba, the Mozambico dramatic dance of Minas Gerais and Holy Cross festival processions, and also in jazz-rock, free jazz and Latin jazz.
奎卡鼓為巴西膜鳴摩擦鼓，演奏時以肩帶將鼓夾於腋下約胸口高度，一手持濕布上下摩擦固: The cuíca is a Brazilian friction membranophone; it is held under the arm at about chest height on a shoulder strap, one hand rubs a damp cloth up and down the wooden or bamboo stick fixed at the centre of the head, and the fingers of the other hand press the head near where the stick is attached. The sound comes from the cloth rubbing the stick, and pitch and timbre change with the outside pressure on the head. A beginner must first master the continuous rubbing motion and the pressing position, then adjust pitch with finger pressure.
奎卡鼓的起源存在爭議，來源指出不同說法將其追溯至被奴役的班圖人，也與安哥拉、西班: The origin of the cuíca is disputed; the source notes that different accounts trace it to enslaved Bantu people, and link it to instruments such as the pwita/kipuita associated with Angola, Spain and Muslim traders. Its construction is the same as the Portuguese sarronca, the Spanish zambomba, the Catalan simbomba and the Balearic ximbomba, showing that similar friction membranophones exist in these regions. Its Hornbostel–Sachs number is 231.11.
奎卡鼓的鼓身通常以金屬、葫蘆或合成材料製成；鼓面為單面，通常以動物皮製成。鼓內中: The cuíca's body is usually made of metal, gourd or synthetic material; the head is single and usually of animal skin. A short wooden or bamboo stick is fixed at the centre inside the drum, perpendicular to the head, its end rosined and rubbed with a damp cloth in playing. The source does not state the materials of other parts such as the shoulder strap and the cloth.
